title: Enneper Minimal Surface
summary: Classical self-intersecting minimal surface with zero mean curvature and cubical parameterization.
description: Discovered by German mathematician Alfred Enneper in 1864 in connection with the Weierstrass-Enneper representation of minimal surfaces. The surface has zero mean curvature at all points ( = 0$), implying it locally minimizes surface area for a given boundary. Its parameterization is polynomial of degree 3, with coordinates given by  = u(1 - u^2/3 + v^2)$,  = -v(1 - v^2/3 + u^2)$,  = u^2 - v^2$.

rights.credit: Enneper minimal surface parametric representation (Alfred Enneper, 1864; Public Domain).

formula: x = u - u³/3 + uv², y = -v + v³/3 - vu², z = u² - v²
latex: x = u - \frac{u^3}{3} + uv^2,\quad y = -v + \frac{v^3}{3} - vu^2,\quad z = u^2 - v^2

title: The Valley of the Shadow of Death (Roger Fenton, 1855)
summary: Stark Crimean ravine strewn with cannonballs beneath rolling barren hills outside Sevastopol.
description: Roger Fenton's celebrated 1855 salted paper print of the barren ravine near Sevastopol, christened 'The Valley of Death' by British soldiers due to the constant Russian artillery barrage during the Siege of Sevastopol. Fenton traveled with a horse-drawn photographic van containing wet collodion darkroom chemicals. The quiet, eerie landscape scattered with round shot beneath a desolate sky makes this one of the most haunting and influential war landscape backdrops in photographic history.
keywords: Valley of the Shadow of Death

rights.credit: Roger Fenton, The Valley of the Shadow of Death, 1855. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gilman Collection. Public domain.
rights.notes: Salted paper print from glass negative.

title: The Great Pyramid and the Sphinx, Egypt (Francis Frith, 1858)
summary: Sublime 19th-century view of the Great Sphinx and Pyramid of Khufu rising from the desert sands of Giza.
description: Francis Frith's iconic 1858 photograph of the Great Sphinx of Giza, partially submerged in sand dunes before the Great Pyramid of Khufu. Frith undertook expeditions up the Nile with an 8x10 wet collodion field camera, battling blinding desert sand, sweltering temperatures inside his darkroom tent, and boiling collodion. His mammoth albumen prints brought the scale and romance of Egyptian antiquity to Victorian audiences. A classic desert monument and ancient landscape backdrop.

rights.credit: Francis Frith, The Great Pyramid and the Sphinx, Egypt, 1858. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain.
rights.notes: Albumen silver print from wet collodion negative.

title: Gyroid Minimal Surface (Trigonometric SDF)
summary: Triply periodic minimal surface with zero mean curvature discovered by Alan Schoen in 1970.
description: The Gyroid is an infinitely connected, non-self-intersecting triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) discovered by NASA scientist Alan Schoen in 1970. It divides three-dimensional space into two congruent, interwoven labyrinthine networks of channels. Its defining nodal approximation equation is $\sin(x)\cos(y) + \sin(y)\cos(z) + \sin(z)\cos(x) = 0$. Rendered here via real-time raymarched signed distance field (SDF) in Three.js.

rights.credit: Gyroid minimal surface nodal approximation (Alan Schoen, 1970; Public Domain).

title: Klein Bottle Figure-8 Immersion
summary: Parametric immersion of the classical non-orientable 2D manifold in 3D Euclidean space.
description: The Klein bottle is a famous two-dimensional topological manifold with Euler characteristic 0 and no boundary. It is non-orientable, meaning a path can reverse an observer's orientation without crossing an edge. Because it cannot be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$ without self-intersection, this parametric Figure-8 immersion maps it into 3D space with a continuous ribbon of self-crossing geometry.

rights.credit: Klein bottle Figure-8 immersion (Felix Klein, 1882; Public Domain).

title: Beech Tree, Forest of Fontainebleau (Gustave Le Gray, c. 1856)
summary: Gnarled roots and dappled canopy of an ancient beech deep inside the primeval Forest of Fontainebleau.
description: Gustave Le Gray's woodland study of an ancient beech tree in the Forest of Fontainebleau, south of Paris. Using his patented dry-waxed paper negative process, Le Gray captured the intricate texture of mossy bark, sprawling root systems, and gentle light filtering through dense leafy canopy. The Forest of Fontainebleau was the sacred sanctuary of the Barbizon school of landscape painters, whom Le Gray knew and influenced. A lush, enchanted primeval forest nature backdrop.

title: The Great Wave, Sète (Gustave Le Gray, 1857)
summary: Pioneering combination-print seascape capturing a rolling Mediterranean wave and dramatic sunlit cloudscape.
description: Gustave Le Gray's masterpiece 'La Vague' (The Great Wave), photographed on the Mediterranean coast at Sète in 1857. To overcome the collodion emulsion's inability to register both bright sky and dark sea in a single exposure, Le Gray printed two negatives together on a single albumen sheet: one timed for the luminous break of the cresting wave, and one exposed for the dramatic backlit clouds. Regarded as the summit of 19th-century marine photography. An iconic coastal seascape backdrop.

rights.credit: Gustave Le Gray, The Great Wave, Sète, 1857. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gilman Collection. Public domain.
rights.notes: Albumen silver print from two glass negatives.

summary: 3D analog of the Mandelbrot set constructed by Daniel White and Paul Nylander using hypercomplex spherical coordinates.
description: The Mandelbulb is a three-dimensional fractal construct developed in 2009 by Daniel White and Paul Nylander. It extends the classic complex Mandelbrot iteration  \mapsto z^n + c$ into 3D using spherical coordinates  \mapsto (r^8, 8\theta, 8\phi) + \mathbf{c}$. title: Chronophotographie géométrique — Homme marchant en combinaison noire
summary: Étienne-Jules Marey's landmark geometrical chronophotography of a man walking in a black suit with white line markers — the historic foundation of optical motion capture.
description: Recorded in 1883 at the Station Physiologique in Paris. Marey dressed his subject in a black velvet bodysuit with bright white reflective stripes along the limbs and joints, exposing the plate intermittently with a rotating slotted disc. This breakthrough reduced human gait to pure kinetic geometry and directly inspired 20th-century motion capture and pose estimation.

title: L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (The Man with the Rubber Head)

description: Produced by Georges Méliès at the Star Film studio in Montreuil (Star Film catalog no. 361–362). Méliès accomplished the camera scale effect by placing himself on a wheeled trolley moving toward the stationary camera against a black velvet background, double-exposed onto the chemist's laboratory set. A foundational milestone in visual special effects, ideal for facial tracking and generative deformation.

title: Menger Sponge 3D Distance Field
summary: Universal curve fractal with infinite surface area and zero Lebesgue volume discovered by Karl Menger in 1926.
description: The Menger sponge is a 3D generalization of the Cantor set and Sierpiński carpet, described by Austrian mathematician Karl Menger in 1926. It is constructed by repeatedly dividing each cube into  \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ sub-cubes and removing the central sub-cube and the 6 face-centered sub-cubes. Its Hausdorff dimension is $\frac{\ln 20}{\ln 3} \approx 2.7268$. Evaluated in Three.js using folded iterative domain distance estimation.

rights.credit: Menger Sponge fractal geometry (Karl Menger, 1926; Public Domain).

summary: Sheer vertical canyon cliffs towering 500 feet over ancestral cliff dwellings in Canyon de Chelly.
description: Timothy H. O'Sullivan's landmark photograph taken during the Wheeler Geological Survey in 1873. The composition frames the ancestral Puebloan White House ruins dwarfed by the striated, colossal 500-foot sandstone ramparts of Canyon de Chelly, Arizona (then New Mexico Territory). O'Sullivan placed his survey equipment and staff at the base to establish monumental scale against the sheer rock face. An archetypal American canyon and desert monolith landscape backdrop.

title: The Flatiron (Edward Steichen, 1904)
summary: Pictorialist twilight view of Daniel Burnham's Flatiron Building reflecting in wet Madison Square pavement.
description: Edward Steichen's iconic nocturnal cityscape of Manhattan's Flatiron Building soaring into the twilight above Madison Square. Steichen created several variant impressions with green, blue, and amber gum bichromate over platinum, blending the sleek geometry of modern American steel-frame skyscraper construction with Whistler-inspired Japanese woodblock composition. Bare branches, wet cobblestones, and the glowing lanterns of horse-drawn cabs create an indelible atmospheric city backdrop.

rights.credit: Edward Steichen, The Flatiron, 1904. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Alfred Stieglitz Collection. Public domain.
rights.notes: Gum bichromate over platinum print.

title: Winter – Fifth Avenue (Alfred Stieglitz, 1893)
summary: Horse-drawn coach plowing through swirling snowbanks during a fierce Manhattan blizzard on Fifth Avenue.
description: Alfred Stieglitz's quintessential winter street scene, captured with a hand-held 4x5 detective camera during a raging snowstorm at Fifth Avenue and 35th Street in New York City. Stieglitz waited three hours in freezing conditions for the coach and team of horses to surge forward through billowing drifts. The photograph marked a revolutionary turning point from stiff studio setups to dynamic, atmospheric instantaneity in American photography. An atmospheric blizzard and turn-of-the-century urban street backdrop.

rights.credit: Alfred Stieglitz, Winter – Fifth Avenue, 1893 (printed 1905). The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Alfred Stieglitz Collection. Public domain.
rights.notes: Photogravure on paper.

title: The Pond—Moonlight (Edward Steichen, 1904)
summary: Pictorialist moonlight landscape across a wooded pond in Mamaroneck, New York, hand-toned in gum bichromate.
description: Edward Steichen's seminal 1904 pictorialist photograph of the moon rising above trees reflecting in a tranquil pond in Mamaroneck, New York. Steichen achieved the subtle nocturnal color tones by manually applying multiple coats of light-sensitive gum bichromate over a platinum print. One of the rarest and most celebrated photographs in American art history, held in the Alfred Stieglitz Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art. An evocative nocturnal forest backdrop.

rights.credit: Edward Steichen, The Pond—Moonlight, 1904 (printed 1906). The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Alfred Stieglitz Collection. Public domain.
rights.notes: Original gum bichromate over platinum and iron print.

title: Torus Knot T(3, 5) Parametric Space Curve
summary: Harmonic topological torus knot winding 3 times longitudinally and 5 times meridionally.
description: In knot theory, a torus knot (p, q)$ is a non-trivial knot that lies on the surface of an unknotted torus in $\mathbb{R}^3$, wrapping $ times around the rotational symmetry axis and $ times through the hole. For coprime =3$ and =5$, the knot possesses pentafoil symmetry and beautiful spatial balance. Rendered with procedural tubular mesh generation and curvature-mapped normals in Three.js.

rights.credit: Torus knot T(3,5) parametric space curve formulation (Public Domain).

description: Carleton Watkins's pristine 1861 mammoth-plate landscape capturing the towering granite buttresses of Cathedral Rock reflected with glass-like stillness in the Merced River. Watkins used an innovative mammoth camera taking 18x22-inch glass plate negatives and custom stereoscopic lenses. The composition balances the towering rock face with riverside cottonwoods, river stones, and crystalline water reflections. A tranquil mountain river and reflection landscape backdrop.

rights.credit: Carleton Watkins, Cathedral Rock, Yosemite, 1861. The Metropolitan Museum of Art / Library of Congress. Public domain.

title: View from the Sentinel Dome, Yosemite (Carleton Watkins, 1865–66)
summary: Mammoth-plate panorama across the high granite peaks, waterfalls, and ancient pines of Yosemite Valley.
description: Carleton Watkins's mammoth-plate albumen print made from a 18x22-inch glass plate negative hauled by mule train to the summit of Sentinel Dome in the high Sierra Nevada. The panoramic view encompasses Nevada Falls, Vernal Falls, Half Dome, and wind-sculpted Jeffrey pines. Watkins's breathtaking Yosemite photographs directly influenced Abraham Lincoln and Congress to pass the 1864 Yosemite Grant Act, creating the first protected public wild parkland. A grand mountainous scenic backdrop.

rights.credit: Carleton Watkins, View from the Sentinel Dome, Yosemite, 1865–66. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Public domain.
